title: The Fly of Egypt and the Bee of Assyria
english: …of the evils no one would pray for has befallen them. For Samaria has been sacked, and the neighboring nations, the Edomites, the Moabites, and the people of Philistia, have overrun Judea as well. So both these and those have suffered many terrible things and have known hard days. Therefore God, he says, will bring days whose like have not yet been, that is, have not yet come upon you, since the time when Ephraim “took away,” that is, tore himself away, from Judah (Isaiah 7:17). And what is this time for us, or what are these days? “The king of the Assyrians,” he says (Isaiah 7:17), that is, Nebuchadnezzar, who sacked Jerusalem, took all Judea by force, and burned the divine temple as well; and of all the savagery fit for a wild beast he left out nothing at all that he is not found to have done against the whole nation.

“And it shall be in that day that the Lord will whistle for the flies, which rule over a part of the river of Egypt, and for the bee, which is in the land of the Assyrians; and they will all come and settle in the ravines of the land, and in the holes of the rocks, and in the caves, and in every cleft, and on every tree” (Isaiah 7:18-19).

He widens the account and describes in detail the onset of the war, and how those who would come against them from time to time would overrun all their land, villages and cities alike. I think it necessary here to tell again what is written in the Second Book of Kings, to make clear exactly what was to come.

Ahaz, to whom the word is now addressed, had a son, Hezekiah; Hezekiah's son was Manasseh, and Manasseh's was Amon. His son was Josiah, a godly man, but he died in this way. Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, left his native land, marched out with his whole army, and pressed on against the land of the Assyrians. Josiah was afraid that he might come against Judea too, bring it under his own hand, and rule over it, and so he wanted to march out against him, although Pharaoh was trying to avoid a battle with him. But in resisting him Josiah died in the war, and the Egyptian took control of the land of the Jews. He grew so strong that he removed Jehoahaz, Josiah's son, from the throne after he had become king, carried him in chains into his own country, appointed Eliakim king, laid tribute on the nation, and demanded a great sum of money.

Then, after Eliakim had reigned over Judea for eleven full years, his son Jeconiah succeeded to the throne, and after him Zedekiah. While Zedekiah held the kingdom, Nebuchadnezzar made war on Judea. He burned all the cities, adding Jerusalem itself to the rest, and took Israel captive, together with the vessels…

title: Why Seek the Dead for the Living?
english: “…who talk emptily, who speak from the belly. Should not a nation go to its God? Why do they seek the dead on behalf of the living? For He gave the Law as a help, so that they might say: Not like this word, for which there are no gifts to give” (Isaiah 8:19-20).

Emmanuel Himself weaves a discourse of instruction for those who have set their hope on Him, who were reckoned among the children and have been given to Him by God the Father (Isaiah 8:18), as to the Savior, Redeemer, and Life-giver, who is able to enlighten them and to free them from every evil. And He draws them wholly away from their ancient habits and their former madness. For it is the custom of idol worshipers to love the oracles of demons and to cling to certain empty-talking necromancers, who say nothing true but simply belch out whatever comes into their heads.

But you, He says, even if someone comes to you and says, “Seek those who speak from the earth,” that is, those who pretend to bring up the dead and to give divinations as if from Hades, or the ventriloquists, who pretend to have certain gods in their belly and so to tell those who come to them what those gods say, do not accept the advice. For they speak only from their own belly, and they are not an understanding nation, such as would seek God and learn something from Him. And say to those who give that advice, “Why do they seek the dead on behalf of the living?”

Do you see how He makes them most sensible? For He not only commands them to turn away from the perversity and madness of those people, but also directs them to become good counselors to those who have gone astray. For say, He tells them, “Why do they seek the dead on behalf of the living?” The reasoning is common sense and human. For what reason could there be in wanting to question those who lie in the earth, or souls that have perhaps come to be in Hades, about people who are still alive?

And in another way too it is utterly ignorant to give heed to necromancy and to the lies of sorcerers, who have a dead mind and, as it were, a heart grown cold. For they do not know the Creator of all; they do not have within them the life-giving Word of God. Besides this, they also busy themselves with dead works. How then can the living, that is, those who have within themselves the life-giving power from above and are rich in the living Word of God, ask the dead about themselves?

So say these things, He says, adding that “He gave the Law as a help,” that is, the Law of the Gospel, so that those who heed it may say: “Not like this word, for which there are no gifts to give.” For those who speak only from their own heart sell falsehood; but the saving and true Law of God, that is…

title: The Shadow Gives Way to the Truth
english: …revealed, those things were held in high praise. So it is also written of Zechariah and Elizabeth: “In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah, and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord” (Luke 1:5-6). In this way, I think, the holy prophets themselves also lived. And indeed the inspired Paul, though he says openly that he had been “blameless as to the righteousness in the Law” (Philippians 3:6), says: “But whatever was gain to me, these things I have counted as loss for the sake of Christ” (Philippians 3:7).

So before the coming of Christ, the Savior of us all, some who were well esteemed for the glories of the Law were strong and in the vigor of youth. But after His appearing and the preaching of the Gospel, the things of the Law have ceased, the shadow has passed over into the truth, and the worship that is in spirit and in truth has been brought in (John 4:23). God therefore does not rejoice over the young men of the Jews (Isaiah 9:17), that is, over those who still show their strength by choosing to live according to the Law. The sacrifices offered through blood are not accepted, nor circumcision of the flesh, nor teachings about washings, nor the idleness of the Sabbaths. But we have been taught, as I said, the way of the life that pleases God.

So, quite rightly, once the shadow came to an end, the young men who live by it are cast off, and the orphans and widows are far from being pitied (Isaiah 9:17). By orphans he means those who, as it were, lack spiritual upbringing and the guidance that comes from teachers. Likewise we say that the widows are souls that have come to lack the power to bear fruit, because they do not have the one who sows and supplies for them all good teachings.

No one would praise the state in which we shall find the people of Israel: without any share in true instruction because of their drunken outrage against Christ. For “their eyes were darkened so that they could not see,” as the psalmist says, and “their backs were bent” (Psalm 69:23), and this “continually,” so that they cannot look at the things above but, as if stooped over, are fixed on earthly things.

They will suffer this, he says, not without cause, but because “all have become lawless and wicked, and every mouth speaks lawless things” (Isaiah 9:17). For how are they not lawless and full of every wickedness, who strove to bring death upon the One who calls them to life, the One who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21), although the Law says plainly, “You shall not kill the innocent and the righteous” (Exodus 23:7)? How has not every tongue of the Jews spoken unjust things? For they cried out against Christ to Pilate, saying, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!” (John 19:15). And, “Unless you kill this man…”
